ann_84.text: Through this part, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 3% to about 27%, and more daytime minutes (112 to 249) clearly raise it from about 1% to about 10%.
Being in California or Washington rather than one of the states the part does not single out raises it to about 12% and 10% (on the training data only).

Montana and New Jersey slightly raise it to about 7%, Texas to about 6%, Maine to about 5% and nine other states to about 3% to 4%, while Vermont, Maryland, Alaska, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania slightly lower it to about 1% and Florida, Wisconsin, Missouri, Alabama and Mississippi to about 2% to 3% (on the training data only).
More evening minutes slightly raise it from about 1% to about 5%, and a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to below 1%.

More voice-mail messages, international minutes, night-time minutes and daytime calls, a longer account, a higher night-time charge and an area code other than 415 slightly raise it, while more international and night-time calls slightly lower it (on the training data only).

ann_85.text: Through this part, customer-service calls (0 to 3) clearly raise the predicted chance of leaving from about 1% to about 13% for the typical customer it acts on (one with 2 customer-service calls and about 129 daytime minutes).

A higher daytime charge (19.07 to 42.40 US dollars) clearly lowers it, and even more so for customers with more than one customer-service call: from about 18% to about 3%, against about 9% to about 3%.
It also clearly lowers it more in New Hampshire: from about 24% to about 1% there, against about 9% to about 3% in most states.

The daytime charge lowers it only while it stays below about 25.31 US dollars: for the typical customer, going from 15.49 to 59.76 US dollars moves it from about 14% to about 3% (on the training data only).
This part acts on 1292 of 4000 customers, 185 of whom left, and for the typical one it slightly raises the chance from about 1% to about 5%.
For that customer, being in New Hampshire raises it from about 5% to about 28% (on the training data only).

ann_86.text: Through this part, customer-service calls clearly add to the predicted chance of leaving from 3 calls upwards: for a typical such customer, going from 0 to 4 calls moves it from about 3% to about 12%.
For the typical customer, calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it to about 4%.
For a typical customer with 3 customer-service calls (one in Idaho), a daytime charge above about 32.03 US dollars slightly lowers it, from about 4% to about 3% (on the training data only).

ann_87.text: Through this part, daytime minutes add to the predicted chance of leaving only once they rise above about 216 minutes: for the typical customer, going from 0 to 271 minutes moves it from about 3% to about 10% (on the training data only).

This part acts on 1002 of 4000 customers, 285 of whom left; for the typical one (a customer in Alabama with about 242 daytime minutes) it raises the chance from about 7% to about 12% (on the training data only).
Across the usual range, more daytime minutes slightly raise it from about 3% to about 6% (on the training data only).
It slightly dampens the daytime-minutes effect in New York: from about 1% to about 18% there, against about 1% to about 21% elsewhere.

ann_88.text: Through this part, account length slightly adds to the predicted chance of leaving only once it rises above about 147, staying at about 3% for the typical customer (on the training data only).

This part acts on 488 of 4000 customers, 77 of whom left; for the typical one (a customer in Oregon with an account length of 163) it slightly raises the chance from about 3% to about 4% (on the training data only).

ann_89.text: Through this part, being in Maryland raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 3% to about 12% (on the training data only).
This part acts on 3918 of 4000 customers, 547 of whom left; for the typical one it lowers the chance from about 12% to about 3% (on the training data only).
Through the linear part, Maryland instead slightly lowers it to about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_90.text: Through this part, being in Louisiana or Missouri slightly raises the predicted chance of leaving to about 3%, and Ohio slightly lowers it, staying at about 3% (on the training data only).

ann_91.text: One small part barely changes the predictions.

ann_92.text: Across the whole model, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 3% to about 27%, and more daytime minutes (112 to 249) clearly raise it from about 1% to about 21%.
A higher daytime charge (19.07 to 42.40 US dollars) clearly lowers it from about 9% to about 3%.
Being in California or Washington rather than one of the states the model does not single out raises it to about 12% and 10% (on the training data only).

Montana and New Jersey slightly raise it to about 7%, Texas to about 6%, Maine to about 5% and eleven other states to about 3% to 4%, while Vermont, Alaska and Pennsylvania slightly lower it to about 1% and Florida, Wisconsin, Alabama, Missouri, Mississippi and New York to about 2% to 3% (on the training data only).

More evening minutes (138 to 266) slightly raise it from about 1% to about 5%, customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it to about 4%, a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to below 1%, and the model ignores evening calls, the evening charge and the international charge.

More voice-mail messages, international minutes, night-time minutes and daytime calls, a longer account, a higher night-time charge and an area code other than 415 slightly raise it, while more international and night-time calls slightly lower it (on the training data only).

ann_84.original: Hypothesis: additive logit backbone (identity node over the 38 direct input->output edges). Formula: 0.107 accountLength + 0.744 internationalPlan - 0.841 voiceMailPlan + 0.297 numberVmailMessages + 1.105 totalDayMinutes + 0.115 totalDayCalls + 0.500 totalEveMinutes + 0.174 totalNightMinutes + 0.050 totalNightCharge (identical to night minutes after z-scoring, net +0.22) - 0.010 totalNightCalls + 0.317 totalIntlMinutes - 0.211 totalIntlCalls - 0.002 areaCode415 + 25 state offsets (|w|<=0.22 per z, e.g. state:46 -0.22, state:47 +0.18, state:4 +0.16). Evidence: exact closed form; sensitivity summary equals |weights|; one-hot offsets: internationalPlan +2.54 logit, voiceMailPlan -1.91 (both match their calibrating offsets on train). numberCustomerServiceCalls has no direct edge: its whole effect runs through the two gates. totalDayCharge is not used directly; totalDayMinutes is (they are identical after z-scoring).
ann_84.proposed: A linear backbone in which an international plan (about 3% to 27%) and daytime minutes (about 1% to 10%) raise the chance of leaving and a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it; state and other usage effects are slight or seen on the training data only.

ann_85.original: Hypothesis (supported): customer-service-calls x low-day-usage interaction. 104 = relu(0.576 + 0.755 CSC + 1.309 relu(0.332 CSC - 0.212) - 0.862 dayCharge - 1.939 relu(1.429 dayCharge + 1.216) + 0.206 state30 + 0.006 state6 + 1.688 h2039), read out 0.617*h104 + 0.688*relu(0.980 h104 - 0.618). Logit grows ~0.7-1.4 per service call and falls with day charge (slope -3.6 per z while 4834 is on), reaching zero above the day-charge median. Evidence (train, 4000 rows): mean contribution 1.13 (0 calls) to 6.97 (6 calls) in the lowest day-charge decile, 0 above p50 for <=4 calls; active on 32% of rows; sensitivity dominated by dayCharge (0.64) and CSC (0.29). For low-call, low-usage customers it cancels the negative part of the linear dayMinutes slope (+1.105 per z), so day usage below p75 has an almost flat net effect. Side inputs: state30 shifts 104 (row effect -0.85..+1.13, mean -0.15 net of its direct edge); 2039 (state9-gated) is active on only 3 train rows (CSC 8-9). Linearising this child alone costs 0.012 train AUC; restoring it alone to the all-linear model gains 0.050.
ann_85.proposed: Customer-service calls with low daytime charge: calls raise the chance of leaving (about 1% to 13% for the customers it acts on), and a higher daytime charge lowers it, more so with more than one call and in New Hampshire.

ann_86.original: Hypothesis (supported): a second service-calls threshold gated off by high day charge. 7506 = relu(-0.687 + 0.739 CSC - 2.266 relu(0.859 dayCharge - 0.133)), read out 1.195*h7506 + 1.451*relu(0.242 + 0.773 h7506) (9029 always on: constant 0.35 plus net slope 2.32 on h7506). Evidence (train): +0.35 constant for 0-2 calls; from 3 calls it adds ~+1.3 logit per extra call when day charge is below its median, much less in p50-75 and nothing above p75 (except 7+ calls). Active on 12.8% of rows. Together with csc_low_day_gate the model matches the empirical pattern: CSC>=4 & day charge <p25 churn 0.90-1.00 (model 0.81-0.84); CSC>=4 & day charge >p50 churn 0.19-0.20 (model 0.20-0.25); CSC 0-3 churn 0.04-0.06 below p75 (model 0.05-0.07). The two gates are largely redundant: linearising either alone costs only 0.012-0.013 AUC, both together 0.063.
ann_86.proposed: A customer-service step from 3 calls upwards (about 3% to 12% at 4 calls), slightly weakened by a daytime charge above about 32.03 US dollars.

ann_87.original: Hypothesis (supported): high-usage hinge. 6238 = relu(-0.508 + 0.769 dayMinutes - 0.018 state34), read out 1.725. Zero for the bottom ~75% of day minutes (z<0.66), +0.36 logit at p75-90 and +1.46 above p90, where churn is 0.49 vs 0.06-0.15 below. summary.text: For a typical customer (one in West Virginia with area code 415, an account length of 100, no international or voice-mail plan, one customer-service call and median usage such as 180 daytime minutes), the model predicts about a 3% chance that the customer leaves, and an international plan clearly raises that to about 27%.
